summaries.headline: States Seek ESSA Waivers Under Trump Administration Push
summaries.summary: The Trump administration is encouraging states to apply for waivers from Every Student Succeeds Act provisions, with Education Secretary Linda McMahon framing the effort as "returning education to the states." Several states have already submitted requests for potentially significant changes to student outcome measurements, school improvement requirements, and federal funding usage, with state leaders citing goals to reduce bureaucracy and free up money for academic initiatives. Advocacy groups are raising concerns that these moves could weaken accountability systems and redirect resources away from English learners and other marginalized student populations.

summaries.headline: California's Literacy Law Faces Implementation Reality Check
summaries.summary: California passed AB 1454 last year to strengthen reading instruction through evidence-based practices, but experience from other states shows legislation alone doesn't change classrooms. Successful states like Rhode Island and Louisiana paired curriculum approval lists with clear quality criteria, educator involvement in material reviews, and transparent messaging about why certain materials meet standards. California's State Board must produce a K-8 instructional materials list by 2027, creating a critical opportunity to learn from states that translated policy ambitions into measurable classroom improvements.

summaries.headline: California Requires Financial Literacy Course for High School Graduation
summaries.summary: California will require high school students to complete a one-semester personal finance course for graduation starting with the class of 2030-31, following the State Board of Education's adoption of curriculum standards. The course covers banking, budgeting, credit management, student loans, investing, and career pathways, with implementation beginning in the 2027-28 school year to align with the state's $1.9 billion CalKIDS college savings program for low-income students. The mandate positions California among a growing number of states recognizing financial literacy as essential preparation for post-secondary success, particularly as student debt and economic complexity continue to challenge young adults.

summaries.headline: SEL Training for Teachers Overlooks Their Own Emotional Skills
summaries.summary: Researchers argue that professional development focuses heavily on teaching students social-emotional skills while neglecting educators' own emotional competencies needed to handle classroom stress. The authors from Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence and University of Virginia propose three practical strategies: regular emotional check-ins with colleagues, creating "emotional safety plans" for high-stress situations, and building school-wide cultures that normalize discussing adult emotions. Schools investing in comprehensive SEL programs may see limited returns if the adults implementing them lack the emotional tools to manage their own responses to daily classroom challenges.

summaries.headline: NYC Plans Literacy Push for Struggling Secondary Students
summaries.summary: Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced plans to expand NYC Reads beyond elementary schools to target middle and high school students reading below grade level, calling it the "next stage" of the city's literacy overhaul. More than 40% of New York City middle schoolers were not considered proficient readers on last year's state tests, and just under half of high school freshmen arrived on campus reading below grade level. The expansion acknowledges that secondary teachers skilled at literary analysis often lack training in foundational reading instruction needed to help struggling adolescent readers catch up.

summaries.headline: Oregon's Short School Year Compounds Chronic Absenteeism Impact
summaries.summary: Oregon teachers say the state's unusually short academic calendar leaves insufficient time to address learning gaps created by persistent student absenteeism, as the state ranked below national averages in math and reading on the 2024 NAEP. The achievement concerns prompted Oregon to overhaul its accountability system, requiring districts to track kindergarten attendance alongside academic proficiency metrics for grades 3, 8, and 9. State data suggest that when official instructional time shrinks, chronic absenteeism becomes even more damaging to student outcomes, creating a compounding effect that hamstrings recovery efforts.

summaries.headline: Michigan Lawmakers Target Teacher Training for Literacy Crisis
summaries.summary: Michigan lawmakers have introduced legislation requiring science of reading training for all K-5 teachers by 2031-32 and mandating teacher preparation programs provide this training before certification. The push comes as just 38.9% of third graders were proficient on state reading tests last year — the lowest in the exam's 11-year history — and only 24% of fourth graders scored proficient on national assessments, ranking Michigan 44th nationally. The legislative package represents a second major attempt to address persistent literacy challenges, coming a decade after the state's 2016 Read by Grade 3 law failed to move performance substantially.

summaries.headline: K-12 AI Adoption Outpaces District Data Infrastructure
summaries.summary: District leaders are rapidly implementing AI tools, with 61% using AI to interpret student data and 56% managing student records, according to Cambium Learning Group research. Six emerging data trends signal the infrastructure shifts needed to support this growth: data platforms are becoming AI-native, governance frameworks are shifting from prevention to enablement, and semantic layers are becoming essential to prevent AI hallucinations. The emphasis on treating data as a managed product with clear ownership and service agreements suggests districts must mature their data operations before AI investments can deliver sustained value.

summaries.headline: Federal Officials Find Jeffco Transgender Policies Violate Title IX
summaries.summary: The Trump administration's Department of Education found that Jefferson County Public Schools' policies allowing transgender students to participate in sports, use bathrooms, and room on overnight trips violate Title IX's sex-based protections. Federal investigators said athletic rosters showed "male students occupy 61 roster positions on girls' sports teams" in Colorado's second-largest district, which serves about 74,000 students. The finding adds Colorado's Jeffco to a growing list of districts facing federal pressure over transgender student policies, following a similar determination against Denver Public Schools for converting a girls' restroom to all-gender use.

summaries.headline: NYC Student Released After 10-Month ICE Detention
summaries.summary: Dylan Lopez Contreras, a 21-year-old student at ELLIS Preparatory Academy in the Bronx, was released Tuesday after spending 10 months in federal immigration custody following his arrest in May 2025. Dylan became the first NYC public school student detained by ICE during Trump's second term, arrested in a federal courthouse hallway after a legal hearing as part of what officials called an unprecedented tactical shift in immigration enforcement. His case drew national attention and advocacy from Mayor Mamdani's administration and Senator Chuck Schumer, highlighting how immigration policy increasingly intersects with school communities serving newly arrived students.

summaries.headline: New Charging Cart Reduces Device Charging Time
summaries.summary: Middle school teachers testing Ergotron's YES Adjusta charging cart found it delivers 40% faster charging speeds than traditional models while taking up significantly less classroom space at 2.4 by 2.1 feet. The pre-wired cart accommodates 24 or 36 devices with adjustable shelves and includes pegboard sides for tool storage, converting into a mobile makerspace when needed. Districts managing hundreds of classroom devices could see meaningful improvements in daily device availability and classroom flexibility with faster turnaround times during instruction.

summaries.headline: Small IT Teams Use Automation to Manage Device Fleets
summaries.summary: District IT teams managing thousands of devices are turning to automated provisioning and zero-touch enrollment to handle one-to-one deployments without adding staff. Longview Independent School District reduced manual device setup time from hours to minutes when managing 13,000 Chromebooks across charter schools, while Riverside Unified's IT team oversees more than 42,000 student devices using scalable management tools. The shift lets technology staff focus on instructional support rather than technical configuration, as manual approaches increasingly fail to meet the demands of large-scale device programs.

summaries.headline: CUNY Expands Early Childhood Teacher Pipeline for NYC
summaries.summary: CUNY officials are ramping up efforts to graduate more early childhood educators as Mayor Zohran Mamdani launches an ambitious expansion of free child care, starting with 2,000 new seats for 2-year-olds this fall and growing to serve all city 2-year-olds within four years. The university system currently enrolls roughly 3,600 students across its 26 campuses in early childhood education programs, and Chancellor Félix Matos Rodríguez has asked college presidents to accelerate their curriculum to push graduates into the workforce faster. The alignment between workforce development and policy expansion could determine whether the city's historic child care promise becomes reality or stalls due to staffing shortages.

summaries.headline: AI Tools Outpace Evidence in K-12 Classrooms
summaries.summary: Stanford researchers analyzed over 1,100 studies on artificial intelligence in K-12 education but found only 20 that rigorously measure AI's impact on student or teacher outcomes. The research shows AI tools can improve performance on math exercises, writing, and programming when students actively use them, but results are mixed when students complete assessments without AI support. Schools are integrating AI into daily practice at scale while operating with a research foundation that remains largely unproven for sustained learning gains.

summaries.headline: Wayne-Westland Replaces 100 Literacy Tools With Coherent System
summaries.summary: Wayne-Westland Community School District tackled inconsistent reading outcomes by consolidating more than 100 fragmented literacy resources into a unified instructional system guided by an 80-member task force of educators. The Michigan district, serving 10,000 students where 63 percent face economic disadvantage, found that despite high teacher effort and significant resource investment, reading instruction varied widely across classrooms and students developed significant gaps by third or fourth grade. The systematic approach to rebuilding Tier 1 instruction suggests that coherence and fidelity matter more than the quantity of available tools when districts seek to improve literacy outcomes at scale.

summaries.headline: Former NYC Chancellor Withdraws From Chicago CEO Search
summaries.summary: Meisha Ross Porter, the former New York City schools chancellor, has withdrawn from the Chicago Public Schools CEO search, leaving interim CEO Macquline King and former East Baton Rouge Parish superintendent Sito Narcisse as the two remaining finalists. Porter told the school board she wanted to "hit the ground running" but felt virtual interviews and limited stakeholder meetings wouldn't allow her to be fully prepared for the role. The Chicago school board expects to hold a special meeting March 30 to discuss the remaining candidates and could select a CEO that day, capping a year-long search process that has included multiple pivots and leaked finalist names.

summaries.headline: AI Education Market Grows Despite Implementation Questions
summaries.summary: The global AI in education market reached $6.4 billion in 2025 and is projected to hit $79.6 billion by 2034, driven by demand for personalized learning platforms and government initiatives across major regions. Higher education leads adoption, while K-12 and corporate training segments expand rapidly as AI tools become more affordable and scalable. The 31% annual growth rate reflects institutional investment in systems that adapt content and pacing to individual student needs, though the market projections say little about actual classroom effectiveness or equitable access across districts.

summaries.headline: New York Schools Remain Nation's Most Segregated
summaries.summary: New York state operates the nation's most segregated traditional public schools, with attendance zones that mirror 1930s redlining maps across New York City, Long Island, Westchester County, and upstate cities like Albany and Buffalo. The state enforces some of the country's strictest residential assignment laws, criminally prosecuting parents who use false addresses to access better schools, with arrests occurring as recently as March 6. These policies create what researchers call one of the most restrictive systems for school access in the country, effectively limiting families' ability to escape assigned districts through open enrollment or school choice options.

summaries.headline: Health Districts Partner With Jail on Health Literacy
summaries.summary: The Hampton & Peninsula Health Districts launched an eight-week health literacy program at Virginia Peninsula Regional Jail, covering 17 topics from medication management to opioid overdose response. Since June, 88 incarcerated individuals have completed the curriculum, with some graduates connecting to substance use treatment and workforce development services after release. The partnership represents a growing recognition that health education during incarceration can address community health disparities and support successful reentry.

summaries.headline: EdTech Cybersecurity Market Projects Massive Growth Through 2034
summaries.summary: The global cybersecurity market for educational technology is projected to grow from USD 36 billion in 2024 to USD 243 billion by 2034, reflecting a 21.2% annual growth rate driven by expanding digital learning platforms and increasing cyber threats targeting schools. Educational institutions face mounting pressure to protect student records, financial data, and academic research as they store larger volumes of sensitive information online and confront more frequent ransomware attacks. The projected six-fold market expansion signals that cybersecurity will consume an increasingly significant portion of education technology budgets over the next decade.

synthesis.topic_title: School Funding Faces Multi-Front Pressure as States Navigate Budget Constraints
synthesis.whats_happening: State lawmakers are advancing modest funding increases that fall short of education advocates' requests, while local communities increasingly reject district budgets at the ballot box. Education leaders across multiple states are shifting from growth strategies to defensive positioning as budget pressures mount.
synthesis.whats_driving: Post-pandemic fiscal realities are colliding with persistent education funding needs, forcing states to balance competing budget priorities. Federal pandemic aid is winding down while districts face ongoing staffing costs and infrastructure demands, creating a funding gap that states are struggling to fill through traditional revenue streams.

The governor on Thursday signed into law the bill that gives Iowa’s K-12 public schools a 2 percent increase in state general funding for the next school year. (Erin Murphy/The Gazette)

DES MOINES — Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds on Thursday signed a bill into law that will give Iowa’s K-12 public schools a 2 percent increase in state funding for the next school year.

This is the first bill Reynolds has signed into law this year.

[Senate File 2201,](https://www.legis.iowa.gov/legislation/BillBook?ga=91&ba=SF%202201) which was passed by the Iowa House and Senate this month, represents a K-12 education spending package of nearly $4 billion, according to an [analysis by the nonpartisan Iowa Legislative Services Agency](https://url.us.m.mimecastprotect.com/s/BMBxCNknBQIZvZyGUmfwIyLCKQ?domain=legis.iowa.gov).

“Together with state, local and federal funds, Iowa schools are estimated to benefit from more than $9.1 billion in total education funding next school year,” Reynolds said at the bill signing.

Reynolds also touted investments in Iowa’s education workforce and increased STEM and work-based learning opportunities.

“These investments and more demonstrate Iowa’s commitment to empowering educators, elevating academic standards and driving accountability to ensure every Iowa student succeeds at school, work and life,” Reynolds said in a statement Thursday.

Iowa Senate Republicans initially proposed a 1.75 percent increase in K-12 state aid, while House Republicans proposed a 2.25 percent increase, before the chambers agreed on the 2 percent increase.

The legislation sets per-pupil funding at $8,148, an increase of about $160 per student. The plan includes roughly $105.9 million in new spending when factoring in other education provisions and represents a 2.7 percent overall increase in general fund support compared to the current budget year, Republican leaders said.

### ‘Slap in the face’

Democrats and public education advocates have argued the funding is insufficient for public schools to maintain their current budgets and that it fails to keep up with inflation, which they say will result in school closures, staffing cuts and larger class sizes.

“Another meager 2 percent increase is a slap in the face to Iowa’s students and public schools,” Jenny Turner, a West Des Moines parent and board president of Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement, said in a news release.

“We are only going to see more programs like Boone’s century-old orchestra program being shuttered. Other districts are moving to four-day school weeks. Staff is being cut across the board, leaving teachers with unmanageable class sizes.”

### \[gaz-ad-2\]

Ten Iowa school districts — Cedar Rapids, Urbandale, Decorah, Cedar Falls, Albia, Belmond-Klemme, Bennett, Keokuk, South Tama and Washington — signed onto an Iowa Citizens for Community Improvement resolution calling for a 5 funding increase for schools.

From the first year under Iowa’s current public school funding formula in 1973 through 2010, general state funding to K-12 public schools increased by an annual average of 5 percent. Since Republicans regained at least partial control of the state lawmaking process in 2011, that annual increase has averaged 2.1 percent. Last year, the funding increased 3 percent.

The Iowa State Education Association President Joshua Brown called the budget approval a “direct hit to educational quality.”

“A 2 percent increase is effectively a cut that forces impossible choices on districts while public funds are diverted to private school vouchers — often for families already enrolled in private education," Brown said in a statement Thursday. "Ultimately, these millions should be used to close the decade-long funding gap in our public classrooms."

Lawmakers on the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee on Thursday unanimously approved an amended version of a bill to reform the state’s school funding formula.

If the bill makes it through the House and Senate, it will be the first time the formula has changed since it was introduced two decades ago.

For years, education leaders, lawmakers and researchers have said the formula does not accurately reflect modern realities of school budgets. In 2024, the Legislature tasked a state research group with studying ways to make the formula more equitable for school districts, and earlier this session the education committee [adapted those recommendations into a bill](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/03/04/lawmakers-draft-overhaul-of-maines-scrutinized-school-funding-formula/).

School district leaders from around Maine supported the reforms [at a public hearing early this month](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/03/09/maine-school-district-leaders-agree-funding-formula-update-is-overdue/).

The original bill included major changes like updating regional salary adjustments to be linked to modern cost-of-living models, altering how special education funding is calculated and factoring the local poverty rate into a district’s ability to pay.

The current formula calculates a district’s ability to pay for its educational expenses based on property tax valuations. The bill proposes adding the rate of economically disadvantaged students into the assessment as a proxy for the local poverty rate. Researchers provided multiple models for how that adjustment would affect the amount of money districts get from the state, integrating the poverty rate at different weights.

Advertisement

Using a 10% weight, the majority of districts would get more state funding under the changes, while 34 districts would see a reduction. Some school leaders who would receive less state funding under the revised formula called on the lawmakers to add a “hold harmless” clause so they won’t have to contend with a huge single-year drop in state subsidy.

Thursday’s amendment, sponsored by Rep. Kelly Murphy, D-Scarborough, integrates the 10% poverty rate. Additionally, every district would be held harmless for three years, which would allow a gradual phase-in of the new funding calculations.

Murphy’s amendment also eliminated several changes to special education that were included in the original version of the bill.

“There’s so much more to know about special ed that we haven’t been able to assess,” she said.

Further, the bill calls on the research group to continue studying the effect of inflation on the funding formula, and other elements of the state’s model.

Committee members praised the researchers and Maine Department of Education for their work on the reports, and celebrated their progress on reforming something that has long been targeted.

“The regional adjustment has not been changed by the Legislature since 2005 when it was initially implemented,” said Rep. Michael Brennan, D-Portland. “Just by the mere fact that we’re doing that, it is a significant step forward.”

DES MOINES — Iowa’s K-12 schools will see a 2 percent increase in general state funding for the coming fiscal year under an agreement reached between legislative leaders and Gov. Kim Reynolds.

House lawmakers Thursday approved an amended school funding bill, while rejecting a Democratic proposal for a larger boost. The agreement falls between earlier proposals this session — [lower than House Republican’s proposed 2.25 percent increase](https://www.thegazette.com/state-government/iowa-house-gop-proposes-higher-k-12-funding-increase-critics-say-its-still-not-enough/) but [higher than the Senate’s 1.75 percent plan](https://www.thegazette.com/state-government/1-75-k-12-funding-increase-panned-by-iowa-education-advocates/) — and [aligns with Reynolds’ budget recommendation released last month](https://www.thegazette.com/state-government/iowa-gov-reynolds-proposes-9-7b-budget-again-drawing-from-state-reserve-funds/).

### \[gaz-ad\]

Lawmakers amended [Senate File 2201](https://www.legis.iowa.gov/legislation/BillBook?ga=91&ba=SF2201) to set per-pupil funding at $8,148, an increase of about $160 per student. The plan includes roughly $105.9 million in new spending when factoring in other provisions and represents a 2.7 percent overall increase in general fund support compared with the current budget year.

The bill passed 58-35, with five Republicans joining Democrats in opposition, and now returns to the Senate for final approval.

Rep. Dan Gehlbach, R-Urbandale, who managed the bill on the House floor, said the plan offers stability for schools while balancing taxpayer concerns.

“This is the largest single appropriation we will make this year,” he said, noting the state will spend nearly $4 billion on K-12 education — more than 40 percent of the entire general fund.

Gehlbach pointed to improving student outcomes, including gains in reading and science scores and declining absenteeism, as evidence current funding levels are effective. Education advocates, however, warned the level falls short of what districts need to keep pace with inflation and rising operational costs, particularly as they face declining enrollment and additional responsibilities tied to state and federal mandates.

### Democrats’ 5% proposal rejected

House Republicans rejected a Democratic amendment that would have increased school funding by 5 percent, or by about $400 per student.

Rep. Heather Matson, D-Ankeny, said districts are struggling with rising costs, including special education deficits, mental health needs and pressures tied to the state’s taxpayer-funded private school Education Savings Accounts program.

![](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/thegazette.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/9/cb/9cbd0c5a-fbba-5a80-b08b-315bac366c40/69a880257f2f3.image.jpg?resize=200%2C150)

“School districts told us they feel like they are in an arms race, because of vouchers,” Matson said, adding the increase would help public schools “climb out of survival mode.”

Republicans opposed the amendment, with Gehlbach estimating it would add $126 million to the state budget. “I respectfully ask the minority party where these funds will be coming from,” he said.

Matson countered that the state has the capacity to invest more, pointing to projections that state revenue will grow by 4.2 percent in fiscal 2027.

### Ongoing divide over school funding levels

Democrats argued the 2 percent increase continues a long-term trend of underfunding public schools.

From 1973, when the current public school funding formula was created, until 2010, general state funding to K-12 public schools increased by an annual average of 5 percent. Since Republicans regained at least partial control of the state lawmaking process in 2011, that annual increase has averaged 2.1 percent. Last year, the funding increased 3 percent.

Districts across the state have reported budget challenges tied to enrollment declines and rising costs, [with some announcing staff cuts, program reductions or building consolidations](https://www.thegazette.com/k/iowa-public-schools-cut-staff-programs-as-enrollment-falls-and-state-funding-fails-to-keep-up-with/). Parents and educators have raised concerns about larger class sizes and fewer course offerings.

“Excellence cannot be sustained on an empty promise,” said Rep. Mary Lee Madison, D-West Des Moines. “We cannot expect world-class results from classrooms held together with duct tape and determination.”

### What the bill does

In addition to the 2 percent per-pupil increase, the legislation:

- Extends property tax relief by having the state cover growth in certain school levies
- Continues state funding for the “budget guarantee,” ensuring districts with declining enrollment receive at least 101 percent of prior funding and preventing tax increases that would otherwise be levied locally
- Provides $7 million for paraeducator and support staff pay — about half the $14 million originally proposed by House Republicans, who say they will continue negotiations with the Senate to secure additional funding.
- Increases transportation equity funding — which provides additional support to districts with high per-pupil busing costs — by 2 percent and caps it at $1 million per district
- Adds a second enrollment count date in January to better reflect student attendance

### Republicans: More funding, fewer students

Gehlbach argued the plan increases resources even as enrollment declines.

He said the bill adds more than $100 million in funding while public school enrollment has dropped 1.5 percent this year to about 473,000 students.

“That demographic reality driven by lower birth rates means fixed costs are spread across a smaller base, naturally boosting dollars remaining per student in the classroom,” Gehlbach said.

The bill also shifts the cost of the “budget guarantee” from property taxpayers to the state, directing an additional $42.2 million to districts with declining enrollment.

He also pointed to long-term trends in school staffing, noting that while K-12 enrollment has declined by 5 to 6 percent over the past decade, total school staff has increased by 11 percent. He said administrative positions have grown even faster.

“I would suggest they do what Iowa has done, and take a hard look at spending and budgeting,” he said.

Gehlbach added that total education funding in Iowa — including state, local and federal sources — exceeds $11 billion annually, or about $24,000 per student.

### \[gaz-ad-2\]

He also defended the state’s ESA program, noting each account is funded at the same $8,148 per-pupil amount while public schools retain more than $1,600 in categorical funding for students who leave. About 42,000 students are using ESAs this year at a cost of roughly $330 million.

“In Iowa, we don’t have public money — we have taxpayer money,” Gehlbach said. “ … We have given parents the ultimate choice on what is best for their child in Iowa. We're not funding the system, we're funding the students.”

### Democrats: Costs rising, flexibility limited

Matson pushed back on claims of administrative bloat, arguing that staffing growth in recent years largely has been in student-facing roles such as special education teachers, paraeducators, mental health supports, English learner instructors, career and technical education teachers and safety personnel — many tied to mandates.

She added that declining enrollment does not automatically translate to proportional cost reductions, since buildings must remain open, buses must run routes and specialized staff must remain available even if a few students leave a grade level.

Matson also argued Republicans overstate available funding by including restricted dollars in total spending figures. Not all education funding can be used for general classroom expenses, she said, pointing to federal programs like Title I that are earmarked for specific student populations.

### Local impacts highlighted

Matson cited examples from across the state to illustrate the impact.

In Boone, she said, a 100-year-old orchestra program is at risk. Urbandale faces a $1.5 million deficit that could lead to 21 job cuts and reductions to music programs. In Fort Madison, she cited school board concerns that “after years of underfunding and the rise in special education deficits and unfunded mandates, our deficits are bleeding us, and we are anticipating that deficit to double by July 1.”

![2faf8589-401f-5d3f-af61-cb4ab4cd2836](<Base64-Image-Removed>)

![](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/thegazette.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/6/44/6446f861-3174-561b-9a3c-93c473211371/699dc11255fb2.image.jpg?resize=200%2C135)

Wright Elementary School second-grader Amara Stevenson (standing, left) smiles as she walks to her seat after speaking Jan. 12 during public comment at the Cedar Rapids Community School District board meeting at the Educational Leadership and Support Center. The district said it needs to trim more than $10 million to ensure long-term financial stability. (Jim Slosiarek/The Gazette)
JIM SLOSIAREK

In her home district of Ankeny, Matson said officials are planning more than $5 million in cuts over the next four years, which could include fewer elective courses, larger elementary class sizes and reduced staffing.

“When Ankeny — a growing district that budgets very conservatively — is facing cuts in the millions, you know something is really wrong,” she said.

Matson also warned that 199 districts could fall under the budget guarantee, potentially increasing pressure on property taxes. While Republicans included state funding to offset those costs, she called it a temporary fix.

“This bill simply doesn’t get us back on track,” she said.

![residents at meeting](https://i0.wp.com/montclairlocal.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Residents-Line-Up-scaled.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)Residents line up to address the Montclair Township Council about a tax abatement for Lackawanna Plaza Tuesday, March 17, 2026. (MATT KADOSH/MONTCLAIR LOCAL)

Montclair’s town council again delayed its decision on a 30-year tax deal for the developer of Lackawanna Plaza, as residents pressed officials to steer money to schools and impose rent control.

The [project proposes](https://montclairlocal.news/2026/02/council-proposes-tax-deal-for-montclairs-lackawanna-plaza-development-seeks-feedback/) 300 apartments, a supermarket and offices on 8.2 acres at the former train station terminal on Bloomfield Avenue. On Tuesday, the council voted to table approval of the financial agreement until March 24. It marks the second delay for the proposed agreement with developer BDP Holdings LLC after the council [did the same](https://montclairlocal.news/2026/02/montclair-council-pauses-lackawanna-plaza-tax-abatement-amid-rent-control-request/) last month.

“We are listening to you, so if we invite you to come in and share questions and comments with us and we just vote right away it almost would seem then that we’re not listening to you or paying attention,” Mayor Renee Baskerville told the full council chambers. “So, I think sometimes when we do go back and give consideration to what you said, it could very well be a good thing.”

## ‘There Will Be Children’

The council voted 5-1 to table. Deputy Mayor Susan Shin Andersen abstained and Third Ward Councilor Rahum Williams voted against the tabling.

Board of Education member Eric Scherzer was among the residents to ask the council to allocate a portion of the tax abatement funds from what is known as payment in lieu of taxes, or PILOT, to the schools. Under the proposed agreement, the municipal government gets 95% of the revenue and the county gets 5% where under a normal taxing arrangement, the school district would get 57% of taxes.

“There will be children in that new building – a fair number of them because, hopefully, they’re affordable – that will be going to our schools,” said Scherzer, who said that he is not speaking for the full school board. “And we need to educate them, and we need money to do that.”

## School Funding

Scherzer was among a handful of residents to ask that PILOT funds be allocated to the schools. Dan Hafetz, a local parent and co-founder of the group Montclair Partnership for Accountability, Clarity and Trust, which on Tuesday published [a report](https://www.mpactnj.org/pilots) on PILOTs and their impact on schools, also urged the council to direct a portion of PILOT monies for the schools.

“Our schools are in crisis right now. And dramatic changes are being made to right the ship,” Hafetz said. “I’m the parent of a child, who attends a school that will be closing in the fall. It’s a decision that I personally do not fight because we have to make sacrifices. The efforts we’re making right now to put our schools on better financial footing being led courageously by Superintendent Turner, I believe, will.”

Michael Hanley, a financial consultant for the township, answered the concerns about the distribution of PILOT monies. Although he did not explain how the schools would benefit.

“The revenue is all coming to the taxpayer regardless of the pocket it happens to be placed in,” Hanley, of NW Financial Group, said. “Other than the 5% that is required to go to the county, the PILOT and the land taxes are entirely entering into the municipal budget, which defers costs.”

![](https://i0.wp.com/montclairlocal.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Michael-Hanley-scaled.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)Michael Hanley, a financial consultant for the township, addresses the town council Tuesday, March 17, 2026. (MATT KADOSH/MONTCLAIR LOCAL)

## ‘Not a Needy Development’

Several residents read to the council a letter from [Joan Pransky](https://montclairlocal.news/2025/10/obituary-joan-ellen-pransky/), a tenants rights advocate from Montclair, who had raised concerns about the project before she died last October.

“The PILOT program was designed to encourage developers to build in what would be considered an undesirable area where developers would likely have trouble renting or selling,” said resident Toni Martin, quoting Pransky. “To secure a PILOT the developer is required to show that its project would not yield an adequate rate of return and would not be economically feasible without the PILOT.”

“While the Lackawanna Plaza site may satisfy the letter of the law being an area in need of development, the intended plan is surely not a needy development and it is certainly not to be built in a needy town,” she added.

## Can Rent Control Be Applied?

William Scott, chairman of the Montclair NAACP Branch’s Housing Committee, asked that rent control be applied to the project.

“Lackawanna Plaza should come under rent control,” Scott said. “Even though there’s a state exemption, you have the capability through negotiating at this point because if the PILOT is something that the developer strongly needs, you have the capability of asking a developer to not take advantage of that exemption.”

Joseph Ragno, an attorney for the township, told the council that he asked such from the developer, David Placek, CEO of BDP Holdings LLC.

“I had that conversation with his counsel. The result of that is that he would be unwilling to agree to such a term,” Ragno said.

Shin Andersen asked if Ragno is aware of any other instance where a town has applied rent control to a project with a PILOT agreement.

“I am not,” Ragno answered. “I do a lot of this work; I have not come across that.”

## PILOT Amounts

Second Ward Councilor Eileen Birmingham said, “I believe PILOT money should go to the schools.”

She also addressed a concern about PILOT contribution amounts, comparing it to the amount of taxes that another supermarket pays.

“We should not expect that a supermarket in Lackawanna Plaza would be paying all of the sudden $1 million in taxes when it’s just in the supermarket phase,” she said.

![PILOT sign](https://i0.wp.com/montclairlocal.news/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/PILOT_Sign-scaled.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)A resident holds up a sign objecting to the proposal for payment in lieu of taxes, PILOT, for the developer of Lackawanna Plaza at the Tuesday, March 17, 2026 township council meeting. (MATT KADOSH/MONTCLAIR LOCAL)

But not all the concerns were about money. David Greenbaum, a former Historic Preservation Commission member, said Lackawanna Plaza is a state, local and national historic landmark.

“That space is a brilliant space that warrants a great use,” Greenbaum said.” And I believe it will be incredibly commercially viable to be used in a number of different ways. And I do not believe it should be demolished as is currently planned.”

Resident Diane Anglin, a supporter of the project, pressed the council to decide.

“If you’re ‘no,’ vote ‘no.’ If you’re ‘yes,’ vote ‘yes,’ but don’t base your vote on what somebody else is doing,” Anglin said. “Your constituents in your area voted you in to represent the people. This kind of soft way of doing governance is not what we voted you in for. Yes, I want Lackawanna, but I want you as our council people to make a decision. This has gone on way too long.”

School districts across Iowa are struggling with budget problems.

Cedar Rapids is considering closing and consolidating several schools as part of a plan to tame a $13 million shortfall. Des Moines is dealing with a $16 million deficit. In Boone, the district discontinued its orchestra.

It’s not rocket science. Rising costs and declining enrollment are sapping education resources. Districts are cutting programs, teaching positions and other spending areas to keep their budgets balanced.

At this time of year, districts hope the Iowa Legislature will receive their distress signals as they decide how much to increase state aid to K-12 schools. Some groups have called for a 5 percent increase, which is a non-starter in our Republican-controlled Legislature.

A 3 percent increase would exceed the 2.7 percent Midwest inflation rate.

But this week, the Iowa Senate approved a paltry 1.75 percent increase in state school funding for regular district operations, a plan that drew nearly universal criticism from education leaders. GOP Sens. Charlie McClintock, Jeff Taylor and Cherielynn Westrich joined Democrats in opposing the plan.

According to the non-partisan Legislative Services Agency, the state’s cost per pupil will increase to $8,133 in Fiscal Year 2027, which starts in July. Overall, regular program aid will decline from $2.177 billion to $2.135 billion. That’s because 208 districts lost enrollment and would see a decrease in per-pupil aid.

Property taxes usually fill that gap. But the Senate bill provides $47.7 million from the state general fund to keep districts’ budgets from shrinking. It’s called the “budget guarantee” and will allow them to spend 101 percent of the previous year’s spending level.

So, at the bottom line, per-pupil funding will increase by $145 in FY 2027. Is that the best we can do?

The Senate funding level doesn’t keep up with inflation, which has become an almost annual tradition since Republicans took over the Statehouse.

Thanks to a series of deep income tax cuts, Iowa is now spending more money than it collects in revenue to the tune of $1.3 billion. Yes, there are surpluses and reserve funds lawmakers can tap, but those sources of funding are dwindling. Republicans also created publicly funded private school scholarships that will cost $350 million in 2027. The Legislature has approved a mountain of edicts but only a molehill of funding.

Pressures from tax cuts and other spending priorities are squeezing public school funding in the annual contest for state funding.

So, this is a problem Republican lawmakers created for public schools, which have been a repeated target in the GOP’s culture war book bans and teaching restrictions.

Gov. Kim Reynolds proposed a 2 percent increase in state school aid. House Republicans have indicated they will not accept a 1.75 percent rate and are likely to spend more.

It’s all about percentages and spreadsheets. But few, if any, Republicans are talking about what public schools really need to educate the citizens and workforce of tomorrow and the resources they need to do the job. And that’s exactly where the focus must be.

local_articles.summary: Bristol Residents Vote Down Education Budget  The Lincoln County News
local_articles.full_content:
![Bristol residents voted to turn down the education budget at the towns annual town meeting on Tuesday, March 17. The school committee is now tasked with reevaluating the budget; residents will make a decision at a special town meeting. (Emily Bracher photo)](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/BRIannual-meeting-2-EB-3col-color-800x533.jpg)

Bristol residents voted to turn down the education budget at the towns annual town meeting on Tuesday, March 17. The school committee is now tasked with reevaluating the budget; residents will make a decision at a special town meeting. (Emily Bracher photo)

The Bristol School Committee will have to reevaluate the $8,359,130.96 education budget for the upcoming fiscal year after residents voted down the proposed figure at the annual town meeting on Tuesday, March 17.

At the beginning of the meeting, a motion was made for the articles related to the education budget, which was an increase of $187,745.38 or 2.3%, to be considered first, rather than at the end of the warrant. What followed was more than two hours of discussion between members of the school and budget committees as well as residents regarding the budget, particularly Article 40 regarding the $332,360.94 system administration line, an increase $97,094.74 or 41.27%.

Housed within the line are the funds for Bristol’s assessment for the superintendent and executive director positions within Johns Bay Coastal Alliance Education Service Center. As of July 1, Bristol and South Bristol will withdraw from AOS 93 to form a two-town education service center.

In its review of the proposal, the budget committee unanimously voted against recommended the system administration line due to the high costs compared to the size of the student body at Bristol Consolidated School.

Many budget committee members and voters also voiced their feeling of being left in the dark throughout the process of Bristol leaving AOS 93 and forming Johns Bay Coastal Alliance.

“It would have been nice to have local control before they hired two people,” budget committee member Jef Howell said.

Fellow budget committee member Alex Beaudet said the committee and many residents believe being asked to vote on funding the positions after the fact takes away from their role in the decision to leave AOS 93.

The motion was made after voters passed education Articles 34-39, a heated conversation starting at Article 40, which asks if the town can be authorized to expend $332,360.94 for system administration. Article 40 was eventually turned down by voters, who then approved Articles 41 through 45.

Both sides of the argument for Article 40 came to bat during this conversation. Multiple budget committee members urged voters to turn down the article and have the school committee revise it.

Katherine Thompson, who serves as the vice chair of the board for Johns Bay Coastal Alliance, expressed her confidence in the creation of two separate upper-level administration roles. She said that she believes that the model the committee has set up for the education service center is “flexible,” and can be organized however to deliver whatever services the school wants.

In regard to the concern about transparency, Thompson said there wasn’t a public vote on the transition because of a “condensed timeline.”

“The dynamics changed very quickly, and the South Bristol and Bristol school boards decided that it was in our best interest to respond to that quickly,” Thompson said.

AOS 93 Executive Director of Finance and Operations Peter Neilson, who hired as the executive director for the education service center, stood up multiple times to reiterate what Thompson said and lay out the model they have planned for the ESC.

“So you employ people, but you have some extra capacity in those people from year to year,” Nielson said. “You have one or two days a week that they could be helping other schools and an education service center can then leverage that and make those people available.”

In response to Nielson’s comment, Beaudet asked to hear from Bristol residents because Nielson isn’t a Bristol taxpayer and “has invested financial interest in this passing.”

A few articles later, residents voted down an amendment to remove the $332,360.94 from the total amount.

“My recommendation is to turn down the amendment, turn down the article itself, and then have the school board make a motion to not consider the rest of the Articles 47 and 48,” moderator Don Means said.

![Bristol budget committee member Alex Beaudet urged voters to turn down Article 40, which asks if the town can be authorized to expend $332,360.94 for System Administration. The article was eventually turned down and residents voted against the education budget, which will now be reevaluated by the school committee to be brought back into discussion at a special town meeting. (Emily Bracher photo)](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/BRIannual-meeting-4-EB-2col-color-800x533.jpg)

Bristol budget committee member Alex Beaudet urged voters to turn down Article 40, which asks if the town can be authorized to expend $332,360.94 for System Administration. The article was eventually turned down and residents voted against the education budget, which will now be reevaluated by the school committee to be brought back into discussion at a special town meeting. (Emily Bracher photo)

A motion was then made to not consider Articles 47 and 48, which are concerned with raising the funds for the education budget.

“So we want to say, no, go back to your school board with South Bristol and figure out a better way, and then come back with a better administrative structure,” Howell said.

After moving past Articles 47 and 48, voters then turned down Article 49, 80-78. The article asked if the school could be authorized to carry forward $125,000 in the facilities and operations reserve fund and to transfer up to $50,000 from unexpended balances to the same fund for a total balance of $175,000.

Voters approved the $59,382.75 for Johns Bay Coastal Alliance Educations Center’s transition from AOS 93. Before the vote, school committee members urged voters to turn down the article because it believes it is unnecessary as the total was already approved by voters as a part of the education budget process.

“The intention was to generate discussion, and we are not afraid of discussion, we welcome discussion,” outgoing Bristol School Committee Chair Darrin Carlucci said. “The town administrator and the select board have all noted that this article is nonbinding. To vote on a nonbinding article that interferes with the school committee’s statutory authority and the legal budget process, we find this troublesome and may create confusion about how the school budget process works under Maine law.

A brief announcement was made during the meeting congratulating Carlucci for his 18 years of service with the school committee, as he did not seek reelection this year.

At one point during the education budget discussion, select board member Paul Yates said that there isn’t as much commotion amongst voters when discussing the budget for trash removal and paving the roads, but then they “beat the living hell” out of the education budget every year.

“I know a lot of people aren’t satisfied with it and paying the taxes and the increase but Jesus Christ, we got to start somewhere to educate,” Yates said.

Before the education budget discussion began, the select board recognized Means for his 35th year as moderator, who received a standing ovation from the crowd.

Michael Melville stepped in as moderator for Articles 3-28.

Voters approved the municipal budget of $3,838,737.92, an increase of $152,694 or 4.05% from last year.

Taxpayers are responsible for raising $1,887,060.56, an increase of $7,727 or 0.41%.

Voters approved the remaining articles with little discussion, budget items including but not limited to the Bristol-South Bristol Transfer Station budget totaling $426,000, an increase of $127,000 or 35%; the budget for the Bristol Mills Dam and Fish Ladder totaling $62,000, a decrease of $89,539 or 83.2% decrease; the Olde Bristol Days budget totaling $15,000, a decrease of $1,000 or 15.9%; the budget for the Central Lincoln County Ambulance Service totaling $279,014.31, a decrease of $31,019 or 10.53% and the budget for Bristol Fire and Rescue totaling $523,389.33, a decrease of $36,610.67 or 6.67.

The recommended reevaluation for the town totaling $350,000 was also approved.

![Moderator Don Means received a standing ovation after the Bristol select board recognized him for 35 years of service. After the towns annual meeting on Tuesday, March 17, the school committee is tasked with reevaluating the education budget after voters turned it down. (Emily Bracher photo).](https://lcnme.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/BRIannual-meeting-1-EB-3col-color-800x533.jpg)

Moderator Don Means received a standing ovation after the Bristol select board recognized him for 35 years of service. After the towns annual meeting on Tuesday, March 17, the school committee is tasked with reevaluating the education budget after voters turned it down. (Emily Bracher photo).

Residents voted in favor of the amendment of the Central Lincoln County Ambulance Agreement without any discussion. The amended interlocal agreement would more clearly define CLC Ambulance as “a quasi-municipal organization” owned and operated by the towns of Bremen, Bristol, Damariscotta, Newcastle, Nobleboro, and South Bristol.

The changes are in the wording so that CLC Ambulance can transition to Maine Municipal Association insurance and also help employees qualify for the Maine Public Employee Retirement system. An example of this is instead of referring to each town as a “party,” the amended agreement refers to those involved as a “town.”

Means took back over at Article 29 and when the meeting ended, gave more thanks for the recognition.

“So over the years, a lot of faces have changed in the town of Bristol, but you’ve treated me spectacularly,” Means said.

Residents took to the polls Monday, March 16 for the election of officers.

Marlie Reny defeated Andrew Fenniman for a three-year term on the Bristol School Committee, the only contested race of the election. Reny received 178 votes to Fenniman’s 144.

Chad Hanna received 272 votes in his uncontested reelection bid for a three-year term on the Bristol Select Board. Laurie Mahan received 282 votes to be reelected for another three-year term on the Bristol Parks Commission.

Incumbent William “Bill” Balicki and James Doherty received 206 and 66 votes, respectively, to fill two seats on the Bristol Planning Board. The terms are for three years each. Benjamin Pendleton did not seek reelection.

A total of 319 ballots were cast.
